newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Quality slide squeezes Ivorian cocoa exporters.
newsitem.headline: Quality slide squeezes Ivorian cocoa exporters.

text.p: Ivorian exporters with insufficient cocoa stocks to meet April and May contracts are facing a shortage of good quality export grade port arrivals, exporters and crop analysts said on Wednesday.
"The quality is slipping and there is little available cocoa," said one large exporter. "Even if beans are large enough the quality is down in some areas."
Some exporters have large stocks, cutting supplies for others, but many warehouses are emptying after a busy main crop season (Oct-April).

Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, is nearing the end of its main crop season (October-April). Beans of export quality - 105 beans per 100 grammes with up to eight percent humidity - are usually harder to find during the midcrop (May-Sept).
Exporters and crop analysts say bean sizes were around 100/100 grammes against 90-95 in early April but stocks had built up in some exporters' warehouses.
"Now we are dealing more and more with midcrop size beans," said the exporter. "Last year, beans were maincrop size throughout the year (Oct-Sept 1995/96) but that could change."
One trader said some exorters had been caught out by a recent cocoa price rise. Others said the Caistab marketing board had not issued sold enough April and May exports contracts to meet demand.
"There is no cocoa and some people have been careless," he said. "Some exporters bought contracts they had no intention of fulfilling but with prices going up their position has changed."

Port cocoa arrivals for 1996/97 tailed off sharply in April but with the total at 970-980,000 tonnes by April 14, against 1.03 million in the record 1995/96 season, overall supplies have been plentiful.

Exporters said some cocoa stored for long periods had gone mouldy. Poor fermentation of some crop by growers meant some beans were "slaty" (coloured), a category outside the sought-after "good fermented" export grade.
"Some have April contracts but not enough main crop quality cocoa," said one. "It is also harder to get export contracts for April and May."

Heavy rains in late 1996 dogged drying of beans by farmers. Exporters held large stocks of cocoa from December to March to in the hope of better prices. Quantites may have deteriorated and been put aside for later sale, industry sources told Reuters.
Upcountry buyers in southern Ivory Coast told Reuters they had stopped coffee buying to concentrate on finding cocoa for exporters.
Buyers stores visited by Reuters contained little cocoa but small stocks of coffee awaiting grading.
Exporters with large port warehouse stocks said they were now shipping remaining main crop cocoa and would wait until late April or mid-May for midcrop cocoa arrivals.
"We have no more stock. We have just shipped out some of the last of our mian crop," said a manager for one of Ivory Coast's largest exporters. "Some is also going to local (processing) factories."

A few exporters' port warehouses recently seen by Reuters contained large stocks of cocoa but most were emptying after a busy season. Cumulative cocoa bean exports before the busy March contract month totalled about 600,000 tonnes.
More recent figures will be published in early May.
Mid crop arrivals could total over 150,000 tonnes, against an unexepectedly large 200,000 tonnes in 1995/96, crop analysts told Reuters. The overall quality of the 1996/97 midcrop was not yet clear.
Ivory Coast aims to process 50 percent of its overall annual cocoa output to add export value and take lower grade midcrop beans off world markets.
One factory at San Pedro seen by Reuters this week had large cocoa and processed product stocks. At least 80 pallets of bagged cocoa was stored under cover outside.
((-- Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90))
